Can you tell me a little bit about the gun violence prevention bills you introduced this week?

Sure. This week we introduced three. The first one is no crime left behind, which is the one that's directly connected to Michigan State. It basically says if you're convicted of any gun related crime, right, felony or misdemeanor, that you are banned from buying a gun for at least three years after you serve your sentence. The man who perpetrated the mass murder at Michigan State had been convicted of a gun related misdemeanor. served his probation, finished that probation, went out and legally bought a gun at one of these big stores and obviously carried out the attack. And so this is responsible in response, excuse me, directly to that. Then we have a bill that looks particularly at a waiting period after you legally buy a gun. It's a pause for a gun safety act, which basically says we looked at all the data of all these folks who buy a gun out of anger, either to hurt other people or hurt themselves. And it goes back to a time years ago when we had a pause. This is a seven day waiting period. You go and buy gun at Walmart at Dunham's. You've legally bought it. You pick it up seven days later. So there's no crimes of passion. Nothing that we've seen like in Atlanta and Highland Park where people were acting out of immediate anger in a middle of a mental crisis. And then the last one is about researching gun violence and basically allowing the CDC finally to research gun violence as a public health issue. Right now gun violence is the number one killer of children under 21. But the CDC is not allowed to study it as a public health issue. And of the top 30 ways that children die in this country, it's the least researched. And we have places right here in Michigan, at University of Michigan, that do this kind of research so that we can get at the root causes and try to deal with this as a society. So those are the three that we announced this week in addition to safe storage, which we announced about a month ago.
